intent: Add a shell-free native Go launcher and fetch path for distroless images (#56)
Go launcher skeleton, JavaLocator and static cross-build

name: JavaLauncherBinary
role: Static Go executable (launcher/) that will run install, fetch and app start without a shell
conditions: Built with CGO_ENABLED=0 so it needs only the kernel; verified running in FROM scratch on amd64 and arm64. A dynamic build would fail in images without a matching loader and libc, with a misleading 'no such file' error

name: JavaLocator
role: Finds the java executable the warmup jar runs on
conditions: Order: explicit path in the app command (never falls back to another JDK if missing), PATH, JAVA_HOME, well-known JDK paths. Empty PATH entries are skipped so a relative ./java is never picked up. Returns empty when none is found, which the callers treat as the fallback

subject: Cross-compiling in Docker
why: Use FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM with GOARCH=$TARGETARCH so the Go compiler runs natively; emulating the target machine for the build is far slower and unnecessary. Test the amd64 binary on an arm64 host only with an image built for that platform

title: Static binary (CGO_ENABLED=0) over a dynamic build
why: A scratch or distroless image may have no loader or libc, or a different one; a static Go binary needs only the kernel, so one file works in every image
alternative: Dynamic build shipping libc in the tools image — rejected: larger, and breaks when the app image's libc differs

title: Locate java by the app's own launch command first
why: An archive is valid only for the exact JDK that runs the app, so the tool must run on that same JDK; a missing explicit path returns no java rather than silently choosing another
alternative: Always prefer JAVA_HOME — rejected: can pick a different JDK than the app uses, so the cache would never match

name: run --format nul
role: Prints the final launch command as argv, each argument followed by a NUL byte, for the native launcher
conditions: Only affects --print. Shell format stays the default for scripts/mnemo-warmup-exec and the Helm chart. Unknown format exits 2. The bad-option fail-open path also honors --format nul so the launcher never receives shell-quoted text

subject: Non-ASCII arguments
why: Checked on gcr.io/distroless/java21-debian12: UTF-8 arguments pass through run --print --format nul unchanged in the default locale and with a UTF-8 locale; covered by scripts/verify-image.sh. The earlier worry about a POSIX locale did not materialise on this image

title: NUL-separated argv over newline, JSON or shell quoting
why: A NUL byte cannot occur in an argument, so splitting on it is unambiguous and needs no parser or shell; shell quoting needs the shell we are removing
alternative: Newline-separated — rejected: arguments can contain newlines. JSON — rejected: extra parse step and failure mode

title: Fail-open parse path keeps the requested output format
why: A bad option must not stop the app; if the fallback printed shell-quoted text the launcher would receive one malformed argument and could not start the app
alternative: Always shell-quote on parse errors — rejected: breaks the launcher exactly when the fallback is needed

intent: Native install, fetch and exec subcommands

name: launcher exec
role: Asks the jar for the final command, then replaces itself with it via syscall.Exec so the JVM is PID 1
conditions: Only a command whose program is named java is probed; anything else starts unchanged. The helper JVM is bounded by a 60 s timeout. Helper failure, timeout, empty or unterminated output all mean: start the original command. With no java anywhere the app cannot start and the launcher exits 127

name: launcher fetch
role: Runs the jar's fetch as a child and swallows failure so a cache problem never blocks the pod
conditions: Exits 0 on a missing java or a failing jar. With --strict the failure propagates (127 for no java, otherwise the jar's status). Difference from the sh launcher, which exits 0 on an old Java even with --strict, because the Go launcher cannot tell an old-Java startup failure from a real strict failure without a version probe

name: launcher install
role: Copies the tools tree into the shared volume, replacing cp -R
conditions: Preserves permission bits; skips symlinks; writes temp files and renames, so a restarted init container can rerun it. The one step with no fallback: a failure exits 1 and the pod waits, because later containers have nothing to run

title: Replace the process with syscall.Exec instead of spawning the app
why: Exec makes the JVM PID 1, so SIGTERM reaches it directly and its exit status is the pod's, with no forwarding code to get wrong and no resident parent
alternative: Spawn a child and forward signals — rejected: needs signal forwarding and reaping logic, and keeps a second process resident

title: Fail open for cache steps; fail loudly only where no fallback exists
why: A cache problem must never stop a valid start, so fetch failures, helper failures and timeouts fall back; install and the final exec have nothing to fall back to and report an error. --strict keeps the jar's failure status
alternative: Treat --strict like the sh launcher (always exit 0 on a missing or old java) — rejected: indistinguishable from a real strict failure without a version probe

intent: Ship the launcher in the tools image and use it in the injector

name: OfflineInjector launcher commands
role: Generated install, fetch, trainer and app containers all run /mnemo-tools/bin/mnemo-launcher; the install init container runs /opt/mnemo-warmup/bin/mnemo-launcher install /mnemo-tools in the tools image
conditions: App: exec -- <original command>. Trainer: jar train ... (a pass-through to java -jar, no fallback). Fetch: fetch ... Removal checks the managed command is the launcher. The Helm chart is unchanged and still uses the sh scripts and cp

name: tools image launcher stage
role: Builds the Go launcher on the build platform and cross-compiles it for the target architecture into /opt/mnemo-warmup/bin/mnemo-launcher
conditions: go test runs for the BUILD platform only; a test binary for another architecture cannot run on the builder, so an amd64 runner building arm64 would fail if tests were cross-compiled. Verified: install works as non-root with a read-only root filesystem and is rerunnable; an emptyDir is 0777, a fresh Docker volume is not

title: Route the trainer through a jar pass-through subcommand
why: The trainer also runs inside the app image via a shell script, so distroless needed it covered; a pass-through keeps one binary for every jar command instead of a subcommand per CLI command
alternative: Add a launcher subcommand per CLI command — rejected: the launcher would duplicate the CLI surface and need a change for every new command

title: Run go test for the build platform, cross-compile only the binary
why: A cross-compiled test binary cannot execute on the builder, so an amd64 runner building the arm64 image would fail; testing natively and cross-building only the shipped binary works on any runner
alternative: Test with GOARCH=$TARGETARCH — rejected: passes on a native build and breaks in multi-arch CI

intent: Verify the launcher on a real distroless Java image

name: verify-image.sh distroless section
role: End-to-end proof on gcr.io/distroless/java21-debian12 (no shell): launcher install, jar build/push, fetch, cache hit, miss, two corrupt archives, unsupported command, exit status, SIGTERM
conditions: Runs once after the JDK loop and uses only the launcher as executable in the app image. Needs network for gcr.io. All 12 checks pass locally on arm64; CI (amd64, image.yml) is the second architecture. Override the image with DISTROLESS_IMAGE

subject: Corrupt archive layers
why: run only compares the archive size with the manifest; fetch re-hashes on download. A same-size zero-filled archive starts plainly because the JVM's own CDS validation rejects it (inferred from the outcome, the JVM log line was not inspected). Archives are mode 0600 owned by the fetching user, so the app must run as the same user

subject: macOS bash 3.2 and set -u
why: Expanding an empty array as "${a[@]}" is an unbound-variable error and, outside $(...), silently ends the script; use ${a[@]+"${a[@]}"} as cleanup() does

title: Prove PID 1 and signals with docker stop on a real distroless image
why: Unit tests stub exec; only a real container shows that the JVM is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM. Exit 143 (128+15) in under the grace period means the signal arrived and the JVM's own shutdown ran
alternative: Assert only on the stubbed exec arguments — rejected: cannot show signal delivery or PID 1

intent: Document the launcher, its limits and the ADR amendment

name: Shell-free reference section
role: docs/reference.md documents mnemo-launcher install, fetch, exec and jar, the injector use, and the known differences and limits
conditions: Limits recorded: fetch --strict propagates failure (the sh launcher exits 0 on an old Java); no Java version probe, so an old Java costs one wasted JVM start; install has no fallback; exec without java exits 127; the trainer needs Java 21+; the helper JVM is stopped after 60 s; cache files are 0600 owned by the fetching user. The Helm chart still needs /bin/sh and is unchanged

name: ADR 0004 amendment
role: Records that shell-free application images are supported by the native launcher, with the rejected alternatives
conditions: Tools image stays busybox because the Helm chart still uses cp and sh; a scratch tools image waits until the chart retires

title: Test the non-ASCII argument worry instead of documenting it as a limit
why: The suspected mangling under a POSIX locale was a guess; a real distroless run showed UTF-8 bytes unchanged, so the claim and its untested workaround were removed and a regression check added
alternative: Document the limit and a JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS workaround — rejected: both unverified, and the workaround would have been advice nobody had run

title: Record the behavior differences from the shell launcher rather than emulate them
why: Matching the sh launcher exactly (fetch --strict exiting 0 on an old Java) needs the version probe we deliberately dropped; stating the difference lets users choose the launcher that fits
alternative: Add a Java version probe to the Go launcher for parity — rejected: contradicts the confirmed no-probe design and adds a failure mode
